# Glossary {.unnumbered}

This appendix is a reference: packages, functions, R syntax, and statistical terms used across the ebook, each with a short, simplified description and the chapter where the fuller explanation lives.

## Packages

| Package | What it's for | First appearance |
|---|---|---|
| base R | Comes with R itself, no `library()` needed: objects, vectors, arithmetic, comparisons, `data.frame()`, basic tests and models. | Chapter 1 |
| `dplyr` | Manipulating data: filtering rows, building new columns, and grouping and summarising. | Chapter 1 |
| `readr` | Reading data files (e.g. CSV) into R. Faster than base R's own version, and doesn't silently guess wrong. | Chapter 2 |
| `here` | Builds a file path from the project folder down to a file, so code runs on any machine. | Chapter 2 |
| `ggplot2` | All the plotting in this book. | Chapter 2 |
| `gtsummary` | Publication-style summary and regression tables. | Chapter 3 |
| `medicaldata` | Supplies `strep_tb`, the 1948 MRC streptomycin trial data. | Chapter 4 |
| `epitools` | Risk ratios and odds ratios with confidence intervals, from a contingency table. | Chapter 5 |
| `broom` | Tidies a fitted model's coefficients and fitted values into a data frame. | Chapter 6 |
| `broom.helpers` | Not loaded directly. `gtsummary`'s `tbl_regression()` depends on it and finds it automatically once it's installed. | Chapter 7 |

## Functions

### Base R: objects, vectors, and data frames

| Function | What it does | First appearance |
|---|---|---|
| `c()` | Combines single values ('scalars') into a vector. | Chapter 1 |
| `class()` | Reports what kind of value an object holds. | Chapter 1 |
| `data.frame()` | Builds a data frame, columns supplied by name. | Chapter 1 |
| `factor()` | Converts a variable into a set of named categories, with levels in a stated order. | Chapter 1 |
| `library()` | Loads an installed package for the current session. | Chapter 1 |
| `install.packages()` | Downloads a package onto this computer. It only needs to be run once per computer. | Chapter 1 |
| `read.csv()` | Base R's own function for reading a CSV file. Superseded by `readr`'s `read_csv()` from Chapter 2 onward. | Chapter 1 |
| `write.csv()` | Writes an object out as a real CSV file on disk. `row.names = FALSE` leaves out R's own row-number column. | Chapter 1 |
| `is.na()` | Tests whether each value is missing. | Chapter 2 |
| `names()` | Lists a data frame's column names. | Chapter 2 |
| `dim()` | Reports the number of rows and columns. | Chapter 2 |
| `head()` | Prints the first few rows of a data frame. | Chapter 2 |
| `substr()` | Extracts characters from a fixed position in a text string. | Chapter 2 |
| `levels()` | Lists a factor's categories, in their current order. | Chapter 3 |
| `relevel()` | Reassigns a factor's reference level to the one named. | Chapter 3 |
| `list()` | Bundles several (different) objects together. | Chapter 3 |
| `nrow()` | Counts the rows in a data frame. | Chapter 2 |
| `set.seed()` | Fixes the sequence of 'random' numbers R uses, so a random draw repeats the same way every time. | Chapter 4 |
| `as.numeric()` | Converts a value to a number; an ordered factor becomes 1, 2, 3, … in level order. | Chapter 6 |

### Base R: summaries and maths

| Function | What it does | First appearance |
|---|---|---|
| `mean()` | Calculates the arithmetic mean. `na.rm = TRUE` drops missing values before calculation. | Chapter 1 |
| `round()` | Rounds a number to a stated number of decimal places. | Chapter 1 |
| `sum()` | Adds values, or counts the number of `TRUE`s when given a logical condition. | Chapter 1 |
| `summary()` | Prints a quick five-number-plus-mean summary of a variable, or an overview of a data frame. | Chapter 2 |
| `median()` | Calculates the median. | Chapter 3 |
| `sd()` | Calculates the standard deviation. | Chapter 3 |
| `IQR()` | Calculates the interquartile range (the 3rd quartile minus the 1st quartile). | Chapter 3 |
| `quantile()` | Reports the value at a stated percentile. | Chapter 3 |
| `table()` | Cross-tabulates one or more categorical variables into counts. | Chapter 3 |
| `prop.table()` | Converts a table of counts into proportions. `margin = 1` divides by row totals, `margin = 2` by column totals. | Chapter 3 |
| `sqrt()` | Calculates a square root. | Chapter 4 |
| `exp()` | Undoes a natural logarithm, used to convert a log-odds coefficient back to an odds ratio. | Chapter 7 |

### Base R: tests and models

| Function | What it does | First appearance |
|---|---|---|
| `t.test()` | A t-test: a confidence interval and p-value for a mean, or for the difference between two means. `paired = TRUE` runs a paired test; `var.equal = TRUE` assumes the two groups share one variance, the same assumption `lm()` makes of a binary explanatory variable. | Chapter 4 |
| `prop.test()` | A confidence interval and p-value for a proportion, or for the difference between two proportions. Uses a continuity correction by default; `correct = FALSE` switches it off. | Chapter 4 |
| `power.t.test()` | Calculates the sample size needed to detect a given difference in means, or the power a given sample size has. | Chapter 5 |
| `power.prop.test()` | The same calculation as `power.t.test()`, for a difference in proportions. | Chapter 5 |
| `wilcox.test()` | The Wilcoxon signed-rank test, a non-parametric alternative to a one-sample or paired t-test, and, given a formula with a two-group factor, the Mann-Whitney (Wilcoxon rank-sum) test, the alternative to an independent-samples t-test. `mu` sets the reference value for a one-sample test; `paired = TRUE` runs the paired version. | Chapter 5 |
| `chisq.test()` | The chi-squared test of association between two categorical variables. `correct = FALSE` switches off its default continuity correction. | Chapter 5 |
| `fisher.test()` | Fisher's exact test. | Chapter 5 |
| `cor()` | Calculates a correlation coefficient. | Chapter 6 |
| `cor.test()` | A correlation coefficient with a confidence interval and p-value attached. | Chapter 6 |
| `lm()` | Fits a linear regression model. | Chapter 6 |
| `coef()` | Pulls a fitted model's coefficients. | Chapter 6 |
| `confint()` | Pulls a fitted model's confidence intervals. For `glm()`, this refits the model repeatedly ('profiling') instead of using a shortcut formula. | Chapter 6 |
| `predict()` | Uses a fitted model to generate a predicted value for a new set of inputs, supplied as a data frame. | Chapter 6 |
| `glm()` | Fits a generalised linear model. `family = binomial` fits a logistic regression, for a 0/1 response. | Chapter 7 |

### `readr`

| Function | What it does | First appearance |
|---|---|---|
| `read_csv()` | Reads a CSV file into a data frame. Faster than base R's `read.csv()`, and doesn't silently convert text columns to factors. | Chapter 2 |
| `write_csv()` | The `readr` equivalent of `write.csv()`. Named alongside `read_csv()` in Chapter 2, but never called in this book's taught code. | Chapter 2 |

### `here`

| Function | What it does | First appearance |
|---|---|---|
| `here()` | Builds a file path from the project folder, so the same code finds its files on any machine. | Chapter 2 |

### `dplyr`

| Function | What it does | First appearance |
|---|---|---|
| `select()` | Keeps only the named columns. Another package, `MASS`, defines a different function with the same name; this book never loads `MASS`, so `select()` always means `dplyr`'s version. | Chapter 1 |
| `glimpse()` | Prints every column of a data frame, its type, and a preview of its values, one row per column. | Chapter 2 |
| `filter()` | Keeps only the rows that match a condition. | Chapter 3 |
| `mutate()` | Adds a new column, or changes an existing one. | Chapter 3 |
| `arrange()` | Sorts rows by one or more columns. `desc()` reverses the order. | Chapter 3 |
| `desc()` | Reverses the sort order inside `arrange()`, high to low. | Chapter 3 |
| `slice()` | Keeps rows by their position. | Chapter 3 |
| `group_by()` | Groups a data frame's rows by one or more variables, so the next step runs once per group. | Chapter 3 |
| `summarise()` | Collapses each group (or the whole data frame, if ungrouped) into a row of summary statistics. | Chapter 3 |
| `n()` | Counts rows, used inside `summarise()`. | Chapter 3 |
| `slice_sample()` | Keeps a random subset of rows. `prop =` states the fraction to keep. | Chapter 4 |
| `pull()` | Extracts one column as a plain vector, not a one-column data frame. | Chapter 4 |
| `case_when()` | Builds a new column from a list of conditions, checked in order. | Chapter 7 |

### `ggplot2`

| Function | What it does | First appearance |
|---|---|---|
| `ggplot()` | Starts a plot, given a data frame. | Chapter 2 |
| `aes()` | Maps a variable from the data onto a visual property in the plot, e.g. x, y, fill, or colour. | Chapter 2 |
| `geom_histogram()` | Draws a histogram of a continuous variable. `binwidth =` sets the width of each bar. | Chapter 2 |
| `geom_bar()` | Draws a bar chart of a categorical variable's counts. | Chapter 3 |
| `geom_boxplot()` | Draws a boxplot. | Chapter 3 |
| `geom_point()` | Draws a scatterplot. | Chapter 3 |
| `labs()` | Sets a plot's axis labels and title. | Chapter 3 |
| `ylim()` | Fixes the y-axis range shown. | Chapter 3 |
| `geom_smooth()` | Adds a fitted line, with a shaded confidence band, over a scatterplot. | Chapter 6 |
| `geom_hline()` | Draws a horizontal reference line at a stated `yintercept`. | Chapter 6 |
| `stat_qq()` | Plots standardised residuals against what a normal distribution would produce, for checking a regression's normality assumption. | Chapter 6 |
| `stat_qq_line()` | Adds the reference line to a `stat_qq()` plot. | Chapter 6 |

### `gtsummary`

| Function | What it does | First appearance |
|---|---|---|
| `tbl_summary()` | Builds a publication-style summary table ('Table 1'). `by =` stratifies it by a grouping variable. | Chapter 3 |
| `all_continuous()` | Inside `list()` or `statistic =`, means 'every continuous variable in this table'. | Chapter 3 |
| `add_p()` | Adds a column of hypothesis-test p-values to a `tbl_summary()` table. | Chapter 5 |
| `tbl_regression()` | Builds a publication-style table directly from a fitted model. | Chapter 7 |
| `tbl_merge()` | Combines two or more `gtsummary` tables side by side, for comparing crude and adjusted models. | Chapter 7 |

### `broom`

| Function | What it does | First appearance |
|---|---|---|
| `tidy()` | Turns a fitted model's coefficients into a data frame, one row per term. `exponentiate = TRUE` converts a logistic model's coefficients to odds ratios. | Chapter 6 |
| `augment()` | Adds each observation's fitted value (`.fitted`) and residual (`.resid`) back onto the original data. | Chapter 6 |

### `epitools`

| Function | What it does | First appearance |
|---|---|---|
| `riskratio()` | Takes an r x 2 table and calculates the risk ratio, with a confidence interval. r is the number of levels in the exposure variable. | Chapter 5 |
| `oddsratio()` | Takes an r x 2 table and calculates the odds ratio. `method = 'wald'` matches the ± 1.96 x SE formula behind a confidence interval built by hand. | Chapter 5 |

## R syntax and operators

| Symbol | What it does | First appearance |
|---|---|---|
| `<-` | Assignment: stores the value on the right in the name on the left. | Chapter 1 |
| `|>` | The pipe. Takes what's on the left and feeds it in as the first input to what's on the right. Read aloud as 'and then'. | Chapter 1 |
| `%>%` | The older pipe, from `dplyr`, before base R had its own. Both can be treated the same. | Chapter 1 |
| `$` | Pulls one named column, or one named piece, out of a data frame or another R object. | Chapter 1 |
| `%in%` | Tests whether each value appears anywhere in a set. | Chapter 1 |
| `==` `!=` | Equal to, not equal to. | Chapter 1 |
| `<` `>` `<=` `>=` | Less than, greater than, and their 'or equal to' versions. | Chapter 1 |
| `''` | Marks a value as text. Numbers, `TRUE`/`FALSE`, and object or column names don't take quotes. `'20'` will be recognised as text in R. | Chapter 1 |
| `` ` `` | A different kind of quoting mark, needed for a column name containing a space or other unusual character. | Chapter 1 |
| `?` | Followed by a function name, opens that function's help page. | Chapter 1 |
| `#` | Starts a comment in an R script: everything after it on the line is ignored when the code runs. | Chapter 1 |
| `#|` | A chunk option, inside a code chunk: sets things like a chunk's label or whether its output shows. | Chapter 1 |
| `NA` | R's code for a missing value. | Chapter 1 |
| `TRUE` / `FALSE` | The two logical values. Always written in full in this book, never abbreviated to `T`/`F`. | Chapter 1 |
| `!` | Negates a condition. `!TRUE` is `FALSE`. | Chapter 1 |
| `&` | Combines two conditions, both must be true. `TRUE & TRUE` is `TRUE`; `TRUE & FALSE` is `FALSE`. | Chapter 1 |
| `|` | Combines two conditions, either must be true. `TRUE | TRUE` is `TRUE`; `TRUE | FALSE` is `TRUE`. | Chapter 1 |
| `::` | Calls a function from a named package directly, without loading the whole package with `library()` first, as in `dplyr::select()`. | Chapter 1 |
| `/` `^` | Divide, and raise to a power: `x^2` is `x` squared. | Chapter 1 |
| `+` | Inside `ggplot2`, joins plot layers together, not arithmetic addition. | Chapter 2 |
| `~` | A formula: separates a response (left) from an explanatory variable (right), as in `t.test(chol ~ gender)`. | Chapter 4 |

## Statistical terms

### Describing data

| Term | What it means | First appearance |
|---|---|---|
| Categorical variable | A variable that puts each observation into one of a fixed set of groups. Nominal categories have no order (`gender`); ordinal categories do (`phq.c`); binary is a two-category special case (`blm.cvd`), even where R has stored it as the numbers 0 and 1. | Chapter 3 |
| Numeric variable | A variable whose values are numbers, in one of two shapes: count (0, 1, 2, 3, ...) or continuous (12.1, 13.5, ...). A binary variable coded 0/1 is categorical, not numeric, whatever class R has stored it as. | Chapter 3 |
| Factor | R's way of storing a categorical variable, as a set of named levels. What class R stores a variable as (`glimpse()`'s `<dbl>`, `<chr>`, or a factor) is a separate question from what the variable statistically is. | Chapter 3 |
| Reference level | The category everything else in a table or model is compared against. In R the default is the first level in a factor. | Chapter 3 |
| Mean, median | Two measures of a distribution's centre: the arithmetic average, and the middle value when sorted. | Chapter 3 |
| Standard deviation (SD) | A measure of a distribution's spread, usually paired with the mean. | Chapter 3 |
| Interquartile range (IQR) | Another measure of a distribution's spread, usually paired with the median. Reported as the range it spans, the first quartile to the third, not as the single number the gap between them makes. | Chapter 3 |
| Skew | A distribution with a longer tail on one side, where the mean and median differ. | Chapter 3 |
| Table 1 | The semi-standard first table of a paper: participant characteristics, often stratified by group. | Chapter 3 |

### Estimation and uncertainty

| Term | What it means | First appearance |
|---|---|---|
| Population | The entire group of individuals or items we want to draw conclusions about. | Chapter 4 |
| Sample | A subset of individuals drawn from the population, which we observe and measure. | Chapter 4 |
| Point estimate | A single number calculated from a sample (e.g. a sample mean or proportion), used as our best guess for the unknown population value. | Chapter 4 |
| Sampling distribution | The theoretical distribution of point estimates we would get if we took infinite independent samples of the exact same size from the population. | Chapter 4 |
| Standard error (SE) | The standard deviation of the sampling distribution. It measures the precision of our point estimate, smaller SE means more precise, and does not describe the variability of individuals in the population, which is what the standard deviation is for. | Chapter 4 |
| Variance | The SD squared. 'Equal variance' between two groups means the same spread in each. | Chapter 4 |
| Central limit theorem (CLT) | The rule stating that if our sample size is large enough, the sampling distribution of the mean will be approximately normal, regardless of the underlying population's shape. | Chapter 4 |
| Confidence interval (CI) | A range of values, built around a point estimate and based on the standard error, that quantifies our uncertainty about the true population parameter. Also known as an 'interval estimate'. | Chapter 4 |
| 95% CI | If we repeated our sampling process indefinitely, 95% of the calculated CIs would contain the true population value. It is incorrect to say 'there is a 95% chance our specific CI holds the true value'. | Chapter 4 |
| Margin of error | The ± part of a CI, half its width. Fixing the margin we want, and the expected SD or proportion, gives the sample size needed to reach it. | Chapter 4 |

### Hypothesis tests and measures of association

| Term | What it means | First appearance |
|---|---|---|
| Null hypothesis | The baseline assumption in a statistical test, typically stating there is no effect, no difference, or no association between variables in the population. | Chapter 5 |
| Alternative hypothesis | The statement a test weighs the null hypothesis against: that there is an effect, a difference, or an association. A test never proves the null hypothesis true; it only asks whether the sample is surprising enough to reject it in favour of the alternative. | Chapter 5 |
| p-value | The probability of observing a result as extreme as, or more extreme than, the one calculated from our sample, assuming the null hypothesis is completely true. As good practice, we should always report point and interval estimates along with p-values. | Chapter 5 |
| Parametric, non-parametric | Parametric tests rely on an assumed distribution, e.g. a t-test relies on the sampling distribution of the mean being roughly normal (not the data themselves). Non-parametric tests make no such assumption and often work on ranks instead (e.g. Wilcoxon tests). | Chapter 5 |
| Paired, independent samples | Paired (or dependent) samples involve measurements linked to each other (e.g. pre/post tests on the same patient, or matched twins). Independent samples involve completely separate, unrelated groups. | Chapter 5 |
| 2x2 (contingency) table | A table summarising the relationship between two binary variables. In epidemiology, exposure is typically on the rows and the disease/outcome is on the columns. | Chapter 5 |
| Risk, risk ratio | Risk is the probability of an event occurring: the number of cases divided by the total group. The risk ratio (or relative risk) divides the risk in the exposed group by the risk in the unexposed group. | Chapter 5 |
| Odds, odds ratio | Odds compare the probability of an event happening to it not happening: the probability divided by 1 minus the probability. The odds ratio divides the odds of the outcome in the exposed group by the odds in the unexposed group. | Chapter 5 |
| Significance level, statistically significant | The cut-off a p-value is compared with, conventionally 0.05. A result with a p-value below it is called statistically significant. | Chapter 5 |
| Type I error, Type II error | A Type I error rejects a null hypothesis that is true (a false positive); its rate is the significance level. A Type II error fails to reject a null hypothesis that is false (a false negative). | Chapter 5 |
| Power, sample size calculation | One minus the Type II error rate: the chance a study detects a real effect of a given size. A sample size calculation sizes a study to reach a target power. | Chapter 5 |
| Multiple testing | Running many tests in one study: at 0.05 each, about one in twenty true null hypotheses comes out significant by chance alone. | Chapter 5 |
| Null value | The mathematical value representing the null hypothesis. For differences (e.g. risk difference), the null is 0. For ratios (e.g. RR, OR), the null is 1. | Chapter 5 |

### Regression

| Term | What it means | First appearance |
|---|---|---|
| Correlation | A statistic ranging from -1 to +1 that measures the strength and direction of association between two continuous variables. | Chapter 6 |
| Pearson's r | A parametric measure of the degree of a strictly linear relationship between two continuous variables. It is highly sensitive to outliers. | Chapter 6 |
| Spearman's rho | A non-parametric measure of the degree of a monotonic relationship, where the variables move in the same direction but not necessarily at a constant rate. It is rank-based and less affected by outliers. | Chapter 6 |
| Response, explanatory variable | What a regression model explains (the response, also called the dependent variable), and what it explains it with (an explanatory variable, also called an independent variable or a predictor). In epidemiological terms, the outcome is the response and the exposure is an explanatory variable. | Chapter 6 |
| Intercept | The fitted line's value at zero. | Chapter 6 |
| Slope | How much the response changes per unit of an explanatory variable. | Chapter 6 |
| Coefficient | The general name for intercept and slope. | Chapter 6 |
| Residual | The vertical distance between an observed value and the model's fitted line. | Chapter 6 |
| R² (multiple R-squared) | The proportion of the response's variation a model accounts for, from 0 to 1. With one explanatory variable it equals the square of Pearson's r. | Chapter 6 |
| Residual standard error | The typical size of a residual, in the response's units: how far the points sit from the line, not how precise the line is. | Chapter 6 |
| F-statistic | A test of a regression model as a whole. With one explanatory variable it answers the same question as the slope's own test. | Chapter 6 |
| Linearity, constant variance, normally distributed residuals | The three assumptions a fitted line's trustworthiness rests on, checked with diagnostic plots. | Chapter 6 |
| Prediction interval | The range for one individual's predicted value, always wider than the CI for the predicted mean. A different quantity from a CI, not a shortened name for one. | Chapter 6 |
| Extrapolation | Using a model to predict outside the range of data it was fitted on. | Chapter 6 |
| Multivariable | Several explanatory variables, one response. Some writers say 'multiple regression' for the same thing. 'Multivariate regression' is a different, formal term for several responses modelled together, not used in this course. | Summary |
| Complete-case | An analysis that keeps only the rows with no missing value on any variable it uses. | Chapter 7 |
| Logistic regression | A regression model for a binary (0/1) response, fitted with `glm(family = binomial)`. It models the log odds of the response, so its exponentiated coefficients are odds ratios. | Chapter 7 |
| Log odds | The natural logarithm of the odds. Unlike a probability it has no upper or lower limit, which is why logistic regression works on this scale. | Chapter 7 |
| Crude, adjusted | An association estimated on its own (crude), against one estimated alongside other variables that might confound it (adjusted). | Chapter 7 |

### Study design and causal language

| Term | What it means | First appearance |
|---|---|---|
| Confounder | A variable that's a common cause of both the exposure and the outcome, distorting the crude association between them unless properly adjusted for. | Chapter 7 |
| Mediator | A variable that sits on the causal path between an exposure and an outcome. Adjusting for one, unlike a confounder, removes part of the effect itself, not a distortion, which is why the same variable can't be treated both ways. | Chapter 7 |
| Adjustment set | The variables chosen, before fitting a model, to adjust an association for. | Chapter 7 |
| Sensitivity analysis | Fitting a model more than one way, on purpose, to see how much a result depends on an assumption that can't be settled from the data. | Chapter 7 |
| Collider bias | Distortion introduced by adjusting for a variable that's a common *effect* of the exposure and the outcome, not a common cause. | Summary |
| Table 2 fallacy | Reading every coefficient in an adjusted regression table as if it had the same interpretation as the one the model was built to estimate. | Chapter 7 |

## Where to look things up

`?` followed by a function name, typed into the console, opens that function's help page, covered properly in Chapter 1. It's usually faster than searching online, and it's always correct for the version of R installed. RStudio also keeps a set of cheat sheets under **Help → Cheatsheets**, one per major package.
